questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The academic ranking of the university was important. It was crucial for me that I could take econ courses at the graduate level. This was one of the universities where this seemed feasible. I also wanted to go to a place I had never been before, and that I was unlikely to travel to otherwise.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The best half year of my life. I had a wonderful exchange!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. The international office (ISSS) was responsive and helpful if I needed anything.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: My courses hadn't shown up in Canvas even though classes were just a day away, so I asked the international office about this. Turns out, this was standard practice at CU Boulder for many professors.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There were student orientations that guided you through a lot of information.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I lived at International Crossroads, which housed 40-50 international and American students. I can recommend this place if it still exists. The people living there are great, and the house cook serves decent all-you-can-eat meals that are included in the rent five days a week. Also, it is located right across the street from the main campus. This place offers semester leases, which is nice because most places in the U.S. offer only leases on a yearly basis. For a single room, it is about $1,450 per month including food, which is decent considering the Boulder housing market. If you have a roommate, the rent goes down significantly. The rooms are furnished, but they aren't luxurious. Although you might see them market themselves as being a Christian institution, you should not worry about that at all. I was worried about it in the beginning as I am not Christian, but they did not try to push anything on me.
I reserved my spot at this place a few months before I arrived, so I did not get much insight to whether it was difficult to find off-campus housing. However, if you are willing to pay the price, you should not be worried about not finding housing.
https://ralphieslist.colorado.edu/
is useful for off-campus housing. Also, CU offers lawyers to look through your rental contract for you for free.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is very expensive to live in Boulder (both on and off campus), and you should expect to pay more than you do in Boulder. 7,000-8,000 DKK is not uncommon to pay for a single room in a shared apartment in Boulder from my experience.

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was unclear how I was supposed to get permission to enroll in classes. Turns out, I had to ask all my professors for permission through email (which I was granted every time).

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I think it differs across apartments. For the economics department, I had to ask my professors for permission directly.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I am not aware. I think the department of the course you want to enroll in can help you.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very successful as I registered for all the courses I wanted. For one of the courses, I was waitlisted until the classes started. At this point, several students dropped the course, allowing me to enroll.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Start researching the courses and the enrollment process early, so you know if you have to ask for permission from professors, which you should do before the enrollment date.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Academically really sound school

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had one 1000-level course (General Psychology), which is the lowest level, and it was indeed quite easy and pedagogical. I also had ECON 4848 – Applied Econometrics, which was really simple if you've encountered regression analysis before. ECON 4626 – The Economics of Discrimination and Inequality is not that difficult, but it requires critical thinking and the exams and papers are graded harshly. ECON 8686 - Labor Economics II is a p.hd. course, but despite of this, the level isn't too difficult given that you have some prior knowledge of applied micro methods and papers.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The classes I had were smaller and more engaging. Student engagement was more encouraged than at UCPH. Also, there were many quizzes, assignments, and exams throughout the semester, which were all a part of the final grade.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PSYC 1001 - General Psychology
ECON 4626 - The Economics of Inequality and Discrimination
ECON 4848 - Applied Econometrics
ECON 8686 - Labor EConomics II

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend ECON 4626 – The Economics of Discrimination and Inequality by Jeffrey Zax and ECON 8686 - Labor Economics II by Brian Cadena. Both encourage critical thinking, and they are both very useful as an economist. The professors are brilliant, and they encourage students to participate actively in the classrooms. Jeffrey Zax, especially, asks a lot of questions to students (he will only pick those who volunteer to answer the questions, however). 
Brian Cadena is really knowledgeable about labor economics and, in particular, immigration.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing much really. I just didn't expect the prices to be that high.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Most things were more expensive than I expected (e.g., food, housing). In general, I think food (both restaurants and groceries) and, in particular, housing is a fair bit more expensive in Boulder than in Copenhagen. 
As an exchange student, there are no student fees, but you still have free and unlimited access to many nice facilities, such as the recreation centers. The main recreation center is huge, and houses a gym, swimming pools (both indoor and outdoor), volleyball courts, badminton courts, basketball courts, indoor soccer court, etc. You also get a free bus card that you can use for both Boulder and Denver (as well as intercity transportation between them)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There is an abundance of clubs and intermural sports teams you can join. I never did either due to scheduling conflicts.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of free events were offered. For instance, free ice skating, free bowling, hiking, free live concerts, college sports games, and free meditation. In general, there were a lot more activities available to students than there are at UCPH!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Hiking or biking is nice as the mountains are so close that you can walk to the trails from campus. The main street in Boulder (the Pearl Street Mall) is beautiful and has a lot of interesting shops and restaurants. It is also great for people watching. Enjoy the sun on one its many rooftops with a view of the mountains.
For day trips, I recommend Rocky Mountains National Park, Red Rocks Amphitheater, Denver, and Colorado Springs (garden of the gods). Colorado is beautiful, and there are many places to explore! Neighboring states such as Utah, New Mexico, and Wyoming (Yellowstone is “just” 8 hours away from Boulder) are also worth a visit if you have access to a car.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: See my answer to the previous question. I did a road trip to Utah with my friends, which was very successful, so I can recommend that if you have a long holiday. Travelling, in general, is recommendable. Denver airport is a little over an hour away from Boulder by bus.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. People are very friendly. I had already done a previous exchange in the U.S., so maybe that is why it was easier for me.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be open to meeting new people and trying new things. There are quite a few welcome events for new students, which is an excellent way to meet locals. You can also talk to them in class or join the clubs. Most are open to playing sports with you in the recreation center if you ask them.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not much. Some Americans talk a lot and can be a bit braggy.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are open to talking and engaging with strangers. In general, the residents were also very open to meeting new people, which I much appreciated.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1.	Get out there and meet people. This is the quickest way to meet new friends. But even if you're not successful initially, you can try again because there are many opportunities for meeting new people throughout the semester.
2.
https://calendar.colorado.edu/
shows a lot of events for students.
3.	Enjoy life! Spend time in the new environment, and do not study all the time.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Show up on the first day of class, or the professors might drop you from the course! 
Also, look up semester bike rentals at the university. They have bikes of good quality that you can rent for around $40-$50 for a semester.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting some wonderful people and growing as a person. It was very fun to study there as well, and the classes were quite rewarding.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Moving into the place I was living, which had a lot of people. However, after attending a couple of dinners, I was quickly comfortable with staying there.
